title: NYC Trash: A study in persistence
summary: Josh and Chuck explore New York City's trash and sanitation system, from the 1650s filth laws and George Waring's 1890s street-cleaning reforms through the 1968 strike, the switch from cans to bags, and the shutdown of Fresh Kills. They cover how much residential and commercial trash the city generates, the DSNY's trucks, workers, pay and union, the mob-run private carting industry and its worker and pedestrian safety problems, waste-to-energy and out-of-state landfill shipping via the marine transfer stations, and the 2024 push to replace black and blue bags with bins. The episode closes with a listener mail story about an arson in Saint Paul.

segments.title: Opening and topic setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on New York City trash and sanitation, noting it follows their earlier USPS episode.

segments.title: Eric Adams and Jessica Tish's cleanup push
segments.summary: The hosts describe the current mayor's cleanup campaign and sanitation commissioner Jessica Tish, whose family is wealthy and who has worked in civil service.

segments.title: Filthy old New York and land made from garbage
segments.summary: Early New York was very dirty, with a 1650s law banning filth and manure in streets. Lower Manhattan and Ellis Island grew from landfill, with Ellis Island growing from three acres to twenty-eight.

segments.title: Tammany Hall and the Department of Street Cleaning
segments.summary: The earlier Department of Street Cleaning was a source of patronage jobs for the Tammany Hall machine, and money meant for cleanup was stolen or diverted.

segments.title: George Waring's cleanup
segments.summary: Union colonel George Waring led street cleaning from about 1895 with a uniformed, military-style hierarchy, a dramatic change from earlier years. He had previously designed the Memphis sewage system. Robin Nagel is mentioned as an NYU professor who acts as an unpaid sanitation anthropologist.

segments.title: Incinerators and closing landfills
segments.summary: Apartment incinerators were banned in 1989, and landfills inside city limits were shut down, ending with Fresh Kills on Staten Island in 2001, which had taken waste from the World Trade Center.

segments.title: Trash cans to bags and manual collection
segments.summary: The city moved from metal cans to trash bags in the 1968 sanitation strike era and in 1971 dropped cans entirely. Lack of alleys means bags are placed on sidewalks, and workers collect them by hand.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break before the discussion of how much trash New York produces.

segments.title: How much trash NYC produces and the DSNY fleet
segments.summary: The city produces about four and a half million tons of residential trash a year. The DSNY collects residential trash two or three times weekly from fifty-nine districts with over two thousand trucks, which drive about four and a half million miles a year.

segments.title: Garbage truck types and equipment
segments.summary: Trucks include dual-bin recycling models, top loaders, and twelve-ton single-bin 'white elephant' trucks. Garbage trucks have dual steering and brake pedals. The DSNY also operates street sweepers, salt spreaders, and snowplows, which are being electrified.

segments.title: DSNY duties beyond trash
segments.summary: The DSNY also handles composting, snow removal, vacant lots, abandoned cars, and abandoned bikes. Graffiti removal was added in 2023, with eight hundred of one thousand backlogged requests cleared in one month.

segments.title: Worker danger and garbage juice
segments.summary: Sanitation work is hazardous because of sharp objects, garbage juice, and compactors. In 1996, worker Michael Hanley died after hydrofluoric acid thrown in regular trash exploded in a compactor hopper.

segments.title: Physical toll and sanitation worker pay
segments.summary: Workers lift heavy cans by hand, and COVID and Ground Zero illnesses took a toll. Teamsters Local 831 represents them, with entry pay about $43,000 rising to about $89,000 after five and a half years, and early retirement with full benefits.

segments.title: Training and driving garbage trucks
segments.summary: Becoming a sanitation worker requires a civil service exam, a CDL, and about a month of training, with a practice obstacle course. Driving in traffic is hard and dangerous.

segments.title: Waste-to-energy and marine transfer stations
segments.summary: Some trash goes to incinerators that now produce energy, but most leaves the city by barge and rail to landfills in Virginia, South Carolina, Ohio, and elsewhere. Five marine transfer stations were built starting in the early 2000s, with odor control and hawk calls to deter seagulls.

segments.title: Where NYC trash goes and lost-item search
segments.summary: Manhattan trash goes mainly to New Jersey, Staten Island trash to South Carolina, and the rest to Pennsylvania and Ohio. A Lost Valuable Search program lets people search a pile at the marine transfer station for lost items for ninety minutes.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the private carting section.

segments.title: Private carting, mob history, and worker conditions
segments.summary: Commercial trash has been handled by private carters since the 1950s, and the Gambino and Genovese crime families controlled much of it until the 1990s. Today's private haulers have weak unions, and drivers earn less than a helper did in 1985. About two hundred fifty private handlers are overseen by the Business Integrity Commission. Private trucks have more pedestrian fatalities than DSNY trucks.

segments.title: Exploitation of day laborers and zoning reform
segments.summary: Some private companies hired unlicensed day laborers, and Mukhtar Diallo was crushed by a truck. A 2019 law divided the city into zones with no more than three companies each and required safety contracts.

segments.title: Bins replacing bags and Harlem pilot
segments.summary: The city plans to replace bags with bins, with smaller wheelie bins for small buildings and dumpsters for large ones, costing about 150,000 parking spots. A Harlem pilot in September 2023 cut rat sightings by 68 percent. Composting is a newer program aimed at food waste.

segments.title: Wrap-up on NYC trash
segments.summary: The hosts close the trash discussion and mention composting and visiting New York.

segments.title: Listener mail: Saint Paul arson
segments.summary: Listener Teagan describes how a roommate who was a firefighter EMT set a couch on fire in the basement of a Saint Paul house in 2019, and the fire was later admitted.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and invite more listener stories, followed by the production credit.
